The way machine learning has typically been used in game playing is to try to build an opponent model, find mistakes in the opponent’s strategy (e.g., folding too often, calling too often, etc.), and exploit those mistakes (51–53). There's no meaningful card counting in hold'em. The only counting is pretty trivial - I think my opponent is going after a flush. There are two spades on the board, he's probably holding two. I have 0. That means there are probably 9 cards remaining with one to come. I have 2 cards, he has 2 cards, there are 4 on the board. That's 52-8 = 46 cards total, and 9 are good for them. So his odds of hitting are about 20%. Unless people are massively overbetting, which is something that only tends to be done by very good and far more frequently by very bad players, the math itself in poker is very negligible. About as fancy as you'll get is preflop blockers - you have A2o and decide to 4-bet an active 3-better since you have a blocker to the range of hands he'd be likely to be willing to go all the way with.

The real skill in hold'em is more strategic. It's about developing a big picture generic strategy that works pretty well. The reason many strong players could do things like profitably put in 1000 hands an hour is because they're not really thinking much while they're playing. They're certainly not soul reading, or getting sick tells. They just have developed out a solid game strategy and only deviate from that on occasion. 1000 hands an hour, as an aside, is somewhere around 2000 decisions an hour, or a decision every 1.8 seconds.

And a big part of the combat of play is finding holes in an opponent's strategy. A really elementary example is how less experienced players play. Many beginning players like to slowplay (feign weakness) with tons of their strong hands because they want to 'keep the other guy in.' But they also like to bluff, and bluff aggressively. And suddenly we have a major problem. That means when a weak player is putting money in the pot, especially earlier in a hand (before they get to the river and realize 'oh shit, I have the nuts and this pot is near empty), it's going to be disproportionately weak.

But the same game is played at a much higher level between good players - and even good players and AIs. So if this AI was imbalanced in even a single way, it's something that could have been devastating to the AI. There are lots of examples there, but they get esoteric and this post is already long enough. But it also gets even more interesting now. The AI itself was not exploitative. In other words, it was not actually looking for weaknesses in the strategies of the humans - it was simply playing 'its game.'

Ultimately not only is this is an AI defeating humans in yet another game of strategy, but it's also an AI defeating humans using a non-exploitative strategy which means it was using only a fraction of its potential for the sake of mathematical soundness, and that's again simply quite remarkable.
